text: I stood outside the Great Hall summoning courage. After six years utterly focused on achieving Warlocke’s robes I had one final test to pass. I hid exhilaration and terror behind my practised serenity. My doubt was a physical companion, so I reminded myself of my laborious academic studies, weapons training, familial support, and any other thought or superstition which might give me hope. Mostly though, I trusted these Warlockes who had taught me. And I trusted our Order.

I twisted the brass knob and pushed through the heavy oaken door. Inside was a heady air of incense and warm humanity and expectation. I skimmed through the forms and formalities. My true attention was on Grand Eye Banks and Master Zindell, looking for clues. We Initiates were here to swallow the Mother’s medicine and ‘journey within’ — and then what? Was our definitive initiation a lesson, a crucible, or the removal of the final veil?

I knelt before the Grand Eye to accept a sip from a silver chalice. The potion tasted foul; I expressed only gratitude and serenity. A bowed head, a paternal grin from old Banks, then I strolled across the ancient parquetry floor to my neat bedding and sat cross-legged.

My fellow Initiates entered after that. Each new entrant wore white robes and the same expression: a subterranean roiling of doubts and desires and speculations. I abandoned them to their own ceremony and lay back. I closed my eyes.

The sounds began first. The quiet chanting of Warlockes and ethereal notes from exotic instruments. Colours began rippling upon my inner eye, vivid imprints of light that soared and spun. I peeked toward Master Zindell. Upon seeing her smiling and swaying, all my fears evaporated.

Now, the ineffable would be experienced, the innermost brought forth.
The medicine clenched in my belly. I released doubt and launched myself forth. My imagination glided on my breath — with each inhalation the future dilated and countless possibilities danced with my intentions and desires. Upon exhaling I drifted into the past; loved ones and tender memories greeted me there. Another indrawn breath saw me centuries hence as an ancient Warlocke; I strode the world of pain and joy on withered legs. That breath’s release saw me playing with my infant sister. I was in awe of her every action and my heart brimmed with love and kinship.

Each experience felt wildly imaginative. Yet each sensation felt more real than the blankets above me. All my body’s senses were aflame and this heat drove into my flesh and fuelled the conflagration of my imagination even further. My deepest intuition said: this is the real-real.

I swept through time like waves lapping across sand. From sitting on my father’s lap; to helping deliver a babe with arthritic hands; from hours beside my mother gazing at shimmering dust-motes; to the pride of Grand Eye Banks taking a creaky knee and bowing as he offered his light-woven throne to me; from the agony of seeing my best friend’s body grow cold; to the ecstasy I achieved with a secret partner whom my vows forbade. My breath flowed back and forth in tidal waves and time danced in spirals like forbidden lovers.
My sister taught me I could change the present with my past awareness.

I was delving into early memories like a gourmand tasting dishes. I had remembered her occasional casual cruelty — that of a capricious child — but my current journeys revealed how these outbursts were truly rare moments standing in contrast to the constancy of her kindness and love. With this new-old certitude our entire relationship transformed. I was suddenly present again and realised this truth was always valid. I had a wonderful little sister.

If past realities were subtly malleable, future one’s were greatly so. I assessed the several threads of desire composing the rope of my intentions, then separated their colours to weave very different living tapestries. The Mother’s potion allowed my imagination to create reality around me, so I applied this tool with great curiosity.

I lived one life of utmost magical dedication: casting spells beyond the conception of most Master Warlockes, wielding power across nations, striding the centuries like a giant. Then in another lifetime I eschewed the isolation of scholarship and played at hedonism with the people of the nearest city. I found love with a fiery-haired acolyte of Afthonia and we raised several wild-eyed children by a lethargic river. Next, I embodied an exhausting life of zealous imagination and constant poverty. Ignoring my mundane concerns to scribe hundreds of plays and stories and letters and treatises; writing on music and love and geometry and mysticism and even botanica and fungi.

I rode these tides for lifetimes that can only have measured in minutes. These vicarious but personal expeditions gave me a nuanced sense of my elder self: the one who the accumulation of time and wisdom might produce. I summoned them like a nearby friend.
As real as my own hand, with my own eyes and a knowing smile, stood before me a wizened elder. They wore my eyes in their well-worn skin. I was greeted with a wave of palpable compassion.

‘If I can be whoever I want,’ I asked my ancient self, ‘How do I know who to choose?’

‘The How is just decisions.’ They replied.

‘Indeed. And the Why?’ I asked, sensing a tendency to mischief.

‘The Why is also self-contained,’ said my inner elder, ‘Each path has its own why.’

‘Hmm, look,’ I said, chuckling at their evasiveness. ‘I might choose career, love, creativity — each with its consequences. But which is best?’

They offered a world-weary grin. ‘Best for who? For what goal? It’s our life Torus.’

‘If it only matters to me, I can do whatever I want. But...’ I reached for something slippery and ineffable. ‘Surely the cosmos has some grand plan I must follow for the highest good?’

Ancient Torus shrugged. ‘Torus, what does your heart say?’

My racing thoughts were as divergent and quarrelsome as ever. My heart felt the rightness of embracing everything: a boundless ‘Yes’. My gut felt…
It felt that living for magical power was petty; living for passion was simplistic; living for creativity was self-indulgent. No single thread felt better than the rest. Even balancing multiple interests felt, intuitively, no better.

I was stumped.

I scanned lifetimes, like a journeyman reading scrolls. I was missing something obvious. I decided I was just navel-gazing about my desires, and so I peeled myself open to vaster possibilities.
That’s when it came for me.

My stomach knotted. Shadows infiltrated everything. A devouring neverness surrounded me like the threatening silence of an enormous tomb. The emptiness was a living entity, and it ravened through my psyche like a bodily assault. It spoke with purest contempt in a snarling basso profundo.

‘You’ve spent a morning gazing at the sun. Now, you sit dazzled and blind.’ It hated me. This entity hated me from within. ‘You make pretty pictures. Where then is the reality of misery and strife?’

I felt an intense revulsion. I yearned for my previously happy ponderings. ‘This is about learning. I’m reaching for higher truths. Leave me.’

‘Bah! Spoken like the self-deluded daydreamer you are. I dare you to look again, Torus.’

Obediently I reviewed my possible futures. Looking closer, I saw that I’d gained Bank’s throne through ruthless self-denial and towering ambition. I saw the friends I ignored and the coldness I endured — that triumph was hollow. I had been a hedonist too, equally callous, plugging up my heart’s empty rooms with children. Selfish. I’d known uninspiring poverty and delusion as an artist. I escaped into my thoughts and fictions at the cost of reality. Again, a corrupted choice.

‘Warlockes work for the good of all,’ I argued, ‘We journey for grand solutions.’

‘Yes,’ it gloated, ‘While children starve outside. While their parents serve the nobility like oxen. How virtuous.’ Its words dripped with disdain and derision.

I dared to look directly at this personification of despair. Again I saw my own face. I couldn’t truly deny this aspect of reality — the abusive husband, the wolf eating its own child, the cancers growing inside beloved elders, the avid delight in watching something burn to ash. This entity had a name: Adversary.

‘I’m good,’ I promised, believing myself, ‘I ignore the dark impulses, I help others.’

‘Yes, I know.’ Its laughter was the gloating of invaders, ‘You also lust after that serving girl. How old is she, really?’ I flushed with shame, hidden under blankets in the Grand Rotunda. ‘Tell me how you really feel about the Gandmorry people, Torus? What if some filthy Gandy married your sister. Would you hug their pale, bloodless children?’

‘Stop it.’ I begged it, revulsion warring with guilt inside me. It knew the excrement deep in my belly.
